title: Independent experts to review how Eagles handled Jalen Hurts’ blood clots, NFL says
content:
Independent medical experts will review the care Eagles quarterback Jalen Hurts received for blood clots, NFL executive Jeff Miller wrote in a Nov. 6 letter to U.S. Sen. Lisa Blunt Rochester (D-Del.). The NFL and the NFL Players Association will jointly select the experts, who will report their findings and recommendations to both sides.

Miller, the NFL’s executive vice president for communications, public affairs and health policy, responded to an inquiry from Blunt Rochester. In the letter, he detailed the NFL’s response to Hurts’ condition and how the league monitors clotting disorders.

“The NFL and the NFL Players Association have agreed to conduct a joint review of the circumstances related to his injury,” Miller wrote, echoing previously reported news. “As outlined by the league and NFLPA’s Collective Bargaining Agreement, mutually agreed-upon independent medical experts will review the matter and share their conclusions and recommendations with both parties. We look forward to sharing more information with you once the joint review is completed.”

“… As a general matter, each club’s medical staff evaluates and treats each individual player, on a case-by-case basis, including in cases of a suspected or confirmed blood clot. The League and Players Association also have several medical committees that review and monitor player injury data closely. For at least the past decade, the NFL has tracked clotting disorders among players every season through a subcommittee of its General Medical Committee, and this information is shared with the NFLPA. Following the ongoing joint review, the League and NFLPA will consider appropriate next steps, including whether this case points to a need for additional league-wide guidance.”

Hurts, 28, told the Eagles’ medical staff Oct. 8 that he had been cleated in the calf four days earlier in a game against the Los Angeles Rams. He flew to London with the team Oct. 9, and an ultrasound the next day revealed a superficial blood clot in his left calf. The Eagles said their medical staff and doctors in London cleared Hurts to play. He played against the Jacksonville Jaguars on Oct. 11 and flew home with the team after the game.

A follow-up ultrasound Oct. 14 showed the clot had moved. The Eagles placed Hurts on injured reserve on Oct. 17. Two days later, the team and his agent, Nicole Lynn, announced that Hurts had deep vein thrombosis and bilateral pulmonary emboli, meaning he also had blood clots in both lungs. Hurts needed blood thinners and was expected to miss the rest of the season.

On Oct. 20, the NFL defended the Eagles’ handling of Hurts’ care, and the NFLPA called for an investigation.

In her Oct. 21 letter to NFL commissioner Roger Goodell, Blunt Rochester asked whether the league has a standard protocol for preventing, detecting and treating blood clots. She also asked who cleared Hurts to play in London, who cleared him to fly home and whether the NFL would review those decisions.

Her husband, Charles Rochester, tore an Achilles tendon playing basketball and died at 52 after blood clots traveled to his heart and lungs.

“I am deeply relieved that Mr. Hurts’s story did not end the way my husband’s did,” Blunt Rochester wrote.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention estimates that up to 900,000 people in the United States are affected by deep vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism each year.

Miller’s response said the NFL will provide additional information “and find ways to support your efforts around raising awareness and improving outcomes related to blood clot disorders.”

“I’m grateful for an update on the NFL’s review of Mr. Hurts’ diagnosis and for information on the league’s efforts to track clotting disorders in its athletes,” Blunt Rochester said Friday in a statement about the NFL’s response. “While I appreciate the NFL’s transparency, I encourage its leadership to use this moment to increase awareness of DVT and PE to better protect its players and support public health.”
